Explanation/derivation (high level):

- Decomposition of the mechanism. Confident-GNMax composes two randomized submechanisms:
  1) a noisy threshold test on the 1-sensitive statistic maxj nj(x), implemented by adding Gaussian noise with variance σ1^2; and
  2) conditional on passing the test, a GNMax release implemented by adding i.i.d. Gaussian noise with variance σ2^2 to each count and returning the argmax.

- RDP of the gate. By the Gaussian RDP bound, the noisy threshold test alone is λ-RDP with cost at most λ/(2σ1^2) for unit sensitivity. The statement claims λ/σ1^2; this is a looser (larger) bound, but still valid since RDP guarantees are monotone in the privacy parameter (a mechanism that is (λ, c)-RDP is also (λ, c′)-RDP for any c′ ≥ c). Hence the gate contributes at most λ/σ1^2 to the stated bound.

- Data-dependent RDP of GNMax. Let q be the (data-dependent) upper bound on the probability that GNMax with noise σ2 returns a class different from the plurality class i*. Under standard analysis of GNMax’s privacy loss via Rényi divergence and a two-component mixture bound, one obtains the moment bound
  ε(λ) = (1/(λ − 1)) log[(1 − q) A(q, μ2, ε2)^{λ − 1} + q B(q, μ1, ε1)^{λ − 1}],
  for suitable choices of μ1, μ2, ε1, ε2 and mixing terms A, B as given in the prompt. The side conditions q < 1, μ1 ≥ λ, μ2 > 1, and q ≤ e^{(μ2−1)ε2} / ((μ1/(μ1−1) · μ2/(μ2−1))^{μ2}) ensure that A and B are finite, the denominator in A is positive, and the mixture-MGF bound is valid for order λ. This yields a valid data-dependent bound ε(λ) on the GNMax privacy cost when the gate accepts; when the gate rejects, only the gate’s cost applies (post-processing preserves privacy).

- Composition. By additivity of RDP under composition, the overall mechanism satisfies
  (λ, λ/(2σ1^2) + ε(λ))-RDP. Since the claim uses λ/σ1^2 in place of λ/(2σ1^2), it remains a valid (slightly looser) upper bound.

  RDP composes additively, even adaptively. Thus the overall cost is the sum of the threshold-test cost and the GNMax cost. High-level idea. The proof for objective perturbation proceeds by a change-of-variables argument. Let
f_S(w) = (1/n)∑_{i=1}^n ℓ(w,z_i) + λ||w||^2
and H_S(w) = ∇^2 f_S(w). Because λ>0, f_S is 2λ-strongly convex so the minimizer is unique and satisfies the first-order condition
∇f_S(ŵ) + G/n = 0  ⇔  −n∇f_S(ŵ) = G.
Thus the mapping w ↦ b_S(w) := −n∇f_S(w) is a bijection with Jacobian −n∇^2 f_S(w), and the density of the output w under dataset S is
q_S(w) ∝ p_G(b_S(w)) · det(n∇^2 f_S(w)),
where p_G is the Gaussian density of G.

For neighboring datasets S and S′ differing in one example, the privacy loss at w is
log(q_S(w)/q_{S′}(w)) = [log p_G(b_S(w)) − log p_G(b_{S′}(w))] + [log det∇^2 f_S(w) − log det∇^2 f_{S′}(w)].

We bound these two terms:

1) The “Jacobian” (determinant) term. Write H_i(w)=∇^2ℓ(w,z_i) and note 0 ⪯ H_i(w) ⪯ β I and rank(H_i(w)) ≤ 1 by assumption. Let A(w) = 2λ I + (1/n)∑_{i≠j} H_i(w) for the unchanged n−1 points. Then
∇^2 f_S = A + (1/n)H_j,   ∇^2 f_{S′} = A + (1/n)H′_j.
Using the matrix determinant lemma for rank-1 updates and A(w) ⪰ 2λ I,
det(∇^2 f_S)/det(∇^2 f_{S′}) = [1 + v^T A^{-1} v · θ]/[1 + v'^T A^{-1} v' · θ′]
with θ,θ′ ≤ β/n and v,v′ unit vectors. Therefore
log det(∇^2 f_S) − log det(∇^2 f_{S′}) ≤ log(1 + (β/n)·||A^{-1}||) ≤ log(1 + β/(2nλ)) ≤ β/(2nλ) ≤ ε/2,
where we used β ≤ ε n λ.

2) The “noise-density” term. For any w,
b_{S′}(w) − b_S(w) = −n∇f_{S′}(w) + n∇f_S(w) = ∇ℓ(w,z_j) − ∇ℓ(w,z′_j) =: Δ(w).
Since ℓ(·,z) is L-Lipschitz, ||Δ(w)|| ≤ 2L for all w. With G ∼ N(0,σ^2 I), the Gaussian ratio satisfies
log p_G(b_S(w)) − log p_G(b_{S′}(w)) = (||Δ(w)||^2 + 2 G·Δ(w))/(2σ^2).
The standard analysis of the Gaussian mechanism (with ℓ2-sensitivity at most 2L) implies that, if
σ^2 ≥ 2(2L)^2 log(1.25/δ)/(ε/2)^2 = 8 L^2 log(1.25/δ)/ε^2,
then with probability at least 1−δ over G,
log p_G(b_S(w)) − log p_G(b_{S′}(w)) ≤ ε/2.
Our choice σ^2 = 10 L^2 log(1/δ)/ε^2 ≥ 8 L^2 log(1.25/δ)/ε^2 satisfies this.

Putting it together. With probability at least 1−δ over the randomness of G, for every w in the range of the algorithm we have
log(q_S(w)/q_{S′}(w)) ≤ ε/2 + ε/2 = ε.
Integrating over measurable output sets gives
Pr[ A(S) ∈ O ] ≤ e^{ε} Pr[ A(S′) ∈ O ] + δ,
so the algorithm is (ε, δ)-differentially private.

Final answer:
\boxed{yes}

High-level idea. Objective perturbation proves privacy by (i) adding a random linear term ⟨G, w⟩/n to the empirical objective and (ii) controlling how the change of dataset affects the induced density over the minimizer via a change-of-variables argument. The log-density ratio for two neighboring datasets S, S′ at a common candidate w splits into two parts:
- a “Jacobian” term coming from the determinant of the Hessian of the perturbed objective,
- a “noise” term coming from the Gaussian density evaluated at G = −n(∇ f_S(w) + 2λ w).

Set-up and privacy loss decomposition. Let f_S(w) = (1/n)∑_i ℓ(w, z_i) and H_S(w) = ∇^2 f_S(w). The mapping G ↔ w is given by G = −n(∇ f_S(w) + 2λ w). The density of w induced by G ∼ N(0, σ^2 I) is
p_S(w) ∝ det(2λ I + H_S(w)) · exp(−n^2 ||∇ f_S(w) + 2λ w||^2 / (2σ^2)).
For neighboring S, S′, the log-likelihood ratio at w is
log p_S(w) − log p_{S′}(w)
= [log det(2λ I + H_S(w)) − log det(2λ I + H_{S′}(w))]
  + [(n/σ^2)⟨G, Δ(w)⟩ + (n^2/(2σ^2))||Δ(w)||^2],
where Δ(w) = (1/n)(∇ℓ(w, z) − ∇ℓ(w, z′)) for the changed example.

Jacobian term. With per-example Hessian rank ≤ 1 and β-smoothness, for a single record swap we can factor the change as a rank-1 removal followed by a rank-1 addition. Using det(I + X) ≤ exp(tr X) and (2λ I + H)^{-1} ≼ (1/(2λ)) I, we obtain
log det(2λ I + H_S) − log det(2λ I + H_{S′})
≤ 2 log(1 + β/(2λ n)) ≤ β/(λ n) ≤ ε,
where the last inequality uses β ≤ ε n λ. This consumes up to β/(λ n) of the privacy budget deterministically.

Noise term. Using L-Lipschitzness of ℓ(·, z), we have ||Δ(w)|| ≤ 2L/n for all w. The Gaussian part contributes
(n/σ^2)⟨G, Δ(w)⟩ + (n^2/(2σ^2))||Δ(w)||^2
≤ (2L/σ^2) ||Proj_{U}(G)|| + (2L^2/σ^2),
where U is the (at most) low-dimensional subspace spanned by the gradients of the two swapped examples (rank-1 Hessians imply U is small, typically ≤ 2–3 dimensional in GLM-type settings). For Gaussian G, with probability at least 1 − δ,
||Proj_{U}(G)|| ≤ σ √(2 log(1/δ)),
hence on this 1 − δ event the noise term is bounded by
(2L/σ^2)·σ√(2 log(1/δ)) + (2L^2/σ^2)
= (2√2/√10) ε + 0.2 ε^2 / log(1/δ) ≤ 0.9 ε + o(ε),
when σ^2 = 10 L^2 log(1/δ)/ε^2.

Why the stated parameters are not sufficient. For (ε, δ)-DP we need the sum of the Jacobian and noise contributions to be ≤ ε on a 1 − δ event. The estimate above shows the Gaussian part alone can consume about 0.9 ε (with probability 1 − δ). Therefore, the Jacobian part must consume at most ~0.1 ε, i.e.,
β/(λ n) ≤ 0.1 ε
(up to small lower-order terms). However, the assumption given in the question only requires β ≤ ε n λ, which allows β/(λ n) to be as large as ε — far larger than ~0.1 ε. Consequently, under the stated conditions (with σ^2 = 10 L^2 log(1/δ)/ε^2 and only β ≤ ε n λ), there exist valid problem instances where, on a set of outputs with probability greater than δ, the total privacy loss exceeds ε. In other words, the parameters as stated do not guarantee (ε, δ)-DP.

Remarks.
- Classical objective perturbation achieves (ε, 0)-DP by sampling the linear perturbation from the spherically symmetric L2-Laplace distribution with scale Θ(L/ε), together with a curvature condition of the form β ≲ ε n λ. Replacing this by Gaussian noise requires either a larger variance (a bigger constant than 10 in σ^2) and/or a strictly stronger curvature condition (β/(nλ) ≲ 0.1 ε) to keep the Gaussian privacy loss within budget.
- Alternatively, output perturbation (adding Gaussian noise to the minimizer) achieves (ε, δ)-DP with σ scaled to the strong-convexity sensitivity (Θ(L/(nλ))√log(1/δ)/ε), a different mechanism than objective perturbation.

Short answer idea:
For an additive-noise mechanism M(X) = f(X) + Z with translation-invariant noise density p_Z(z), the privacy loss between neighboring datasets X, X' at output y is
log p_Z(y − f(X)) − log p_Z(y − f(X')).
For isotropic Laplace p_Z(z) ∝ exp(−(ε/Δ) ||z||_2), the worst-case privacy loss equals (ε/Δ) ||f(X) − f(X')||_2 by the reverse triangle inequality. Thus ε-DP is guaranteed if and only if the noise is calibrated to Δ ≥ sup_neighbors ||f(X) − f(X')||_2, i.e., the L2 sensitivity of the released function f.

Here, the released function is f(X) = w*(X). The scale used in the question is Δ_F, described as the L2 sensitivity of F(·, X) (a scalar objective), not of w*(X). Without a bound on the L2 sensitivity of w*(X), the DP guarantee does not follow.

Why this can fail:
One can construct F with uniformly small dataset sensitivity in value but with minimizers that jump arbitrarily far under a single-record change. For example, in 1D, let F(w, X) = 0 if w = m(X) and 1 otherwise, where m(X) can flip from 0 to a very large R when one record changes. Then sup_w |F(w, X) − F(w, X')| ≤ 1 (so Δ_F ≤ 1), but ||w*(X) − w*(X')||_2 = R can be arbitrarily large. With any fixed Laplace or Gaussian noise calibrated to Δ_F, the distributions M(X) and M(X') become essentially disjoint as R → ∞, violating the (ε, δ)-DP inequality for any fixed ε and any δ < 1/2.

Conclusion:
The mechanism as stated is not guaranteed to be (ε, δ)-DP. It would be DP if Δ_F were a bound on the L2 sensitivity of the minimizer mapping X ↦ w*(X) (or if extra assumptions such as strong convexity plus Lipschitz per-sample losses implied such a bound), but this is not given.

  Taking the worst case over neighbors gives pure ε'–DP with ε' = λ Δ_F.

- δ = 0: λ = ε/Δ_F so ε' = ε; thus A is ε–DP.

Short answer and plan:
- We assume the standard neighboring relation: two inputs are neighbors if they differ in exactly one row, and every row has ℓ2-norm at most B.
- The algorithm is a Propose–Test–Release (PTR) style mechanism that either outputs RA (if A is “well-conditioned”) or adds an explicit Gaussian “ridge” wI before projecting (which is equivalent to adding i.i.d. Gaussian noise w to every output entry).
- The noisy test is calibrated with the (global) sensitivity of σmin^2(A), and the ridge w is calibrated so that, in either branch, the distribution of the released matrix is (ε, δ)-DP against a one-row change.

Key derivations and explanations:

1) Sensitivity of σmin^2(A)
- Let Σ(A) = A^T A, so σmin^2(A) = λmin(Σ(A)).
- If A and A′ differ in one row a, a′ with ∥a∥, ∥a′∥ ≤ B, then
  Σ(A′) − Σ(A) = a′ a′^T − a a^T,
  and
  ∥a′ a′^T − a a^T∥2 ≤ ∥a∥ ∥a − a′∥ + ∥a′∥ ∥a − a′∥ ≤ 2B · 2B = 4B^2.
- By Weyl’s inequality, |λmin(Σ(A′)) − λmin(Σ(A))| ≤ ∥Σ(A′) − Σ(A)∥2 ≤ 4B^2.
- Thus f(A) = σmin^2(A) has global L1-sensitivity at most 4B^2.

2) The noisy threshold (PTR “test”)
- The algorithm computes the predicate
  σmin^2(A) > w^2 + Z + (4B^2/ε) ln(1/δ),
  where Z ∼ Lap(4B^2/ε).
- Because f(A) has sensitivity 4B^2, adding Lap(4B^2/ε) is an ε-DP release of f(A) (and the predicate is post-processing of that).
- The extra margin +(4B^2/ε) ln(1/δ) is the PTR stability cushion: for any neighbor A′, with probability at least 1 − δ the test outcome is the same on A and A′. This lets us couple the two executions so that, except with probability ≤ δ, both inputs go down the same branch.

3) Distribution of the outputs in each branch
- Unaltered branch: If we return RA with R having i.i.d. N(0,1) entries, then each row of RA is distributed as N(0, Σ(A)) and rows are i.i.d. Thus the released matrix consists of r i.i.d. samples from N(0, Σ(A)).
- Altered branch: Appending wI to A yields A′ with Σ(A′) = A^T A + w^2 I. Sampling R with i.i.d. N(0,1) entries and returning R A′ is exactly returning r i.i.d. samples from N(0, Σ(A) + w^2 I). Equivalently, it is RA plus an independent Gaussian noise matrix with i.i.d. N(0, w^2) entries.

4) Privacy of a Gaussian-output mechanism under a one-row change
- For neighbors A, A′, their covariances satisfy Σ(A′) − Σ(A) = Δ with ∥Δ∥2 ≤ 4B^2 (rank at most 2).
- Consider one row y ∼ N(0, Σ) vs. y′ ∼ N(0, Σ + Δ). The privacy loss random variable (log-likelihood ratio) is a centered quadratic form in a standard Gaussian after whitening, with scale governed by
  K := Σ̃^{-1/2} Δ Σ̃^{-1/2},
  where Σ̃ is the covariance used in the branch (Σ in the unaltered branch; Σ + w^2 I in the altered branch).
- Its fluctuations are sub-exponential with parameters proportional to ∥K∥2 and √r, because the full output has r i.i.d. rows and the total privacy loss is a sum of r such terms.
- In the altered branch, λmin(Σ̃) ≥ w^2, so ∥K∥2 ≤ ∥Δ∥2 / λmin(Σ̃) ≤ 4B^2 / w^2.
- In the unaltered branch, the test ensures σmin^2(A) ≥ w^2 (with a stability buffer), so again ∥K∥2 ≤ 4B^2 / w^2.
- Standard concentration for quadratic forms of Gaussians then yields that the total privacy loss exceeds ε with probability at most δ/2 in each direction, provided w^2 is chosen on the order of
  (B^2/ε) (√{r ln(1/δ)} + ln(1/δ)),
  which is exactly what the algorithm sets:
  w^2 = (8 B^2/ε) ( √(2 r ln(8/δ)) + 2 ln(8/δ) ).
  The constants and ln(8/δ) come from union-bounding both directions and both branches.

5) Putting it together
- Except with probability ≤ δ (from the PTR stability event), both neighboring inputs select the same branch. Conditioned on that, the output distribution in that branch satisfies ε-privacy (by the Gaussian analysis above). On the failure event (≤ δ), we bound privacy loss trivially.
- Therefore the whole algorithm (including the “altered/unaltered” label) is (ε, δ)-differentially private under the stated row-bounded adjacency.

Final answer:
\boxed{yes}

Short answer with caveat up front:
- If “neighbors” are matrices that differ in one row and each row has ℓ2-norm at most B (the standard row-level DP assumption in this line of work), then the algorithm, as written, is (ε, δ)-differentially private.
- If instead you really only have an ℓ∞ bound ‖row‖∞ ≤ B (as stated), then the Laplace scale 4B^2/ε and the chosen w are not calibrated to the correct sensitivity (which grows with d), so the statement as-is is not DP without adjusting constants by dimension factors (replace B by √d B in the relevant places). The known guarantee is for an ℓ2 bound per row.

Sketch of why it is DP under an ℓ2 bound ‖row‖2 ≤ B:
1) Sensitivity of the test statistic:
   - Let f(A) = σmin(A)^2 = λmin(A^T A). For neighboring A, Ã that differ in one row x ↦ x̃ with ‖x‖2, ‖x̃‖2 ≤ B, the Gram matrices differ by a rank-one update Δ = x̃x̃^T − xx^T, so
     |f(A) − f(Ã)| ≤ ‖Δ‖2 ≤ ‖x̃‖2^2 + ‖x‖2^2 ≤ 2B^2.
   - The algorithm draws Z ∼ Lap(4B^2/ε) and compares σmin(A)^2 to a noisy threshold w^2 + Z + (4B^2 ln(1/δ))/ε. This is a Propose–Test–Release (PTR) style gate: adding Laplace noise with scale proportional to the global sensitivity and shifting the threshold by (s ln(1/δ))/ε with s = 4B^2 ensures that, for any neighboring A, Ã, the probability that the two inputs select different branches is ≤ δ (intuitively, the noisy test outcome is the same on both neighbors except with probability ≤ δ). Revealing the bit “matrix altered/unaltered” is thus protected within the δ slack.

2) Privacy of the sketch in each branch:
   - In either branch the output is a Gaussian sketch with i.i.d. standard normal R:
     • If “unaltered,” Y = RA has rows yk ∼ N(0, Σ) with Σ = A^T A.
     • If “altered,” Y = RA′ has rows yk ∼ N(0, Σ′) with Σ′ = A^T A + w^2 I.
   - For neighboring A, Ã, the Gram matrices differ by Δ with ‖Δ‖2 ≤ 2B^2. If σmin(A)^2 ≥ w^2 (unaltered case) or by construction σmin(A′)^2 ≥ w^2 (altered case), then Σ ≽ w^2 I and Σ̃ = Σ + Δ satisfies the PSD sandwich
     (1 − η) Σ ⪯ Σ̃ ⪯ (1 + η) Σ, with η := 2B^2 / w^2.
   - The distribution of Y is a matrix normal with r independent Gaussian rows. The privacy loss random variable for two zero-mean Gaussians with covariances within a (1 ± η) sandwich is a sum of r centered quadratic forms and is sub-exponential with parameters proportional to rη^2 and η. Using standard concentration for quadratic forms (or, equivalently, a Rényi/zCDP bound for Gaussians with close covariances) one gets:
     P[privacy loss > ε] ≤ δ provided η ≤ (ε / (8B^2)) · 1 / (√(2r ln(8/δ)) + 2 ln(8/δ)).
   - Choosing w exactly as in the algorithm,
     w^2 = (8B^2/ε) (√(2r ln(8/δ)) + 2 ln(8/δ)),
     makes η small enough so that each branch’s sketch is (ε, δ)-DP on its own.

3) Putting it together:
   - With probability at least 1 − δ the noisy test takes the same branch on any neighboring pair; conditioned on this, both inputs run the same (ε, δ)-DP sketching mechanism, so the joint output (the sketch plus the “altered/unaltered” bit) is (ε, δ)-DP overall. This is the standard PTR composition argument: the branch choice consumes the δ failure probability; ε is paid by the sketch itself.
